0: When a new model is released, everyone's first instinct is to download it and try it. But once it comes to your own business the questions get concrete: can it handle our business problems? Can it tell what a customer is asking? Do we even need a model this large?
1: So before choosing an open model, be clear about the job to be done.
2: When handling contracts, classifying them, extracting amounts and dates, or generating summaries all call for different abilities. Once the goal is clear you can go to the model hub and know which models fit better.
4: When a business team raises a requirement they usually do not say “we need a classification model” or “we need an information-extraction model”; they describe the problem from the business side, for example “heap me pull the key information out of the contracts” or “reply to users' questions automatically”.
5: The first step in model selection is turning those business requirements into model tasks. Once the task is settled you can judge what kind of model is needed.
6: To decide which model task a requirement belongs to, start from two angles:
8: By the model's working goal, common tasks fall into these categories:
13: Produce new text, images, audio and so on from the input
16: Judge which category the input belongs to
19: Pull the needed information out of the raw data and output it in a given format
22: Find relevant items among a set of candidates and rank them by relevance
23: “Find the best matches and order them”
25: Judge future or unknown outcomes from existing data
28: Different data types need different processing and internal structures, so dedicated models are needed. The common data types are:
42: Processes continuous image and sound information
44: Also note whether the input and output involve only one kind of data. When both are the same type, the model task is classified by that type.
45: For example, image in and image out is an image task. When input and output involve two or more data types it is a multimodal task. Common multimodal tasks include speech-to-text, where the input is speech and the output text; and visual question answering, where the input is an image plus text and the output is text.
46: In practice, look first at the ultimate goal of the business problem, then at the input and output data types. Examples:
48: Once the model task is found, model selection begins. ModelScope offers several ways to filter models; the methods below are worth following.
50: ModelScope tags every model with a task type. On the model hub page:
51: 1. Choose “Models” to enter the browsing page;
52: 2. In the filter bar on the left, choose “Task type”;
53: 3. Choose the corresponding task category (for example “text classification”).
54: The platform then lists the models tagged with that task. This is the most direct way to filter and is recommended first.
56: When the task tag still leaves too many candidates, narrow the field with other tags in the “Framework” and “Other” columns on the left:
57: Framework: filter models for a specific framework such as PyTorch or TensorFlow;
58: Licence: for commercial use, filter for permissive licences such as Apache 2.0 or MIT;
59: Architecture: filter for architectures such as llama, qwen3 or deepseek_v2;
60: Language: choose the languages the task needs — Chinese, English, Japanese, Korean and so on.
62: If you know the exact task or model name, type the keyword into the search box and search, for example “OCR”.
64: ModelScope also tracks how popular models are. The indicators worth looking at are:
68: Reflects how often a model is used overall. More downloads usually means the model has been validated in more scenarios
70: Reflects how much users approve of the model. More favourites suggests better quality or scenario fit
72: Recently updated models usually have better performance or more complete ecosystem support. A model updated long ago may have compatibility problems
74: How quickly issues and discussions are answered, and how lively they are, indirectly reflects the model's maintenance state
75: The platform can sort the filtered models by downloads or likes; the sort basis can be chosen in the top right of the model hub, where you can also see when a model was updated.
76: Community activity must be checked on the model card page, where you can see the number of community exchanges.
77: General models usually have far more downloads than vertical-domain models, so comparing raw numbers across domains means little; compare within the same kind of task.
79: When working with large models one question comes up often: should you choose a general large model, or a specialised model trained for a specific task?
80: Each has its own traits; the choice mainly depends on the task type, the amount of data, inference speed and deployment cost.
82: A general large model is usually pre-trained on a large, multi-domain corpus and can handle many kinds of task: text classification, content generation, information extraction, question answering and so on. It is not optimised for one specific task but aims to be usable in more scenarios.
83: Advantages: one model handles many tasks, and usually only the prompt needs adjusting to make it do different work. For tasks with little data, few-shot or zero-shot attempts can come first, without necessarily preparing lots of labelled data.
84: Drawbacks: general models usually have many parameters and therefore demand a lot of compute. The bigger the model, the more VRAM and compute inference takes, and in high-concurrency scenarios inference speed and deployment cost must be considered too. On some fairly clear specialist tasks a purpose-trained model may perform better.
85: General large models suit scenarios where tasks are varied, where you are still exploring, or where there is not yet enough data to train a specialised model. If you need to validate a new application direction quickly, using a general model directly is usually the convenient choice.
87: A specialised model is trained and optimised for one kind of task or one domain. Models for text classification, OCR, speech recognition or object detection can all be seen as specialised models.
88: Advantages: because the model is optimised for a specific task and usually does not have to handle many unrelated ones, it holds up better on inference speed, resource use and task quality. For applications with fairly fixed tasks you can also train the model further on your own data to fit your business better.
89: Drawbacks: a specialised model's scope is relatively narrow; switch tasks and it may no longer be usable directly. A text-classification model, for example, cannot be used as-is for text generation. If the business requirements change, the original model may need retraining or adjustment. And if a system uses many different specialised models, their versions and deployment environments must be managed separately.
90: Specialised models suit scenarios where the task is clear, the business requirements are fairly stable, and inference speed, resource use or deployment cost matter. If you have accumulated good training data, a specialised model is usually easier to optimise for the concrete task.
92: Real projects do not have to choose between a general large model and a specialised one; the two are often used together.
93: In smart customer service, for example, a general model can first understand the user's question and what they want to solve; once the task is identified it goes to the corresponding specialised model.
94: In practice, start from the task itself. If the task is still vague, or many kinds of problem must be handled at once, lean towards a general model; if the task is already clear and speed, cost or stability matter, then consider a specialised model.
96: A business system usually uses more than one model. Depending on how complex the task is, one model can do all the work, or several models can be combined with each handling one stage. In an intelligent document-processing system, for example, going from document input to final output may pass through document classification, OCR, layout analysis, table recognition and information extraction:
97: In such a system each model handles a different task. Multi-model setups usually share these traits:
98: Each model handles one independent task. For example the OCR model recognises text, the layout model judges where elements are, and the extraction model pulls the needed content from the recognition output.
99: If one stage performs poorly, only that stage's model needs replacing, without reworking the whole system. Tasks with no dependencies can run in parallel, cutting the overall processing time.
100: Use a large model for tasks that need high accuracy, and a lightweight model for stages that need speed and are simple.
101: Multi-model setups also bring a hand-off problem: the output format of one model must be parsed correctly by the next, which means thinking about the data formats between models when designing the system. For example, OCR outputs text blocks with coordinate information, while an extraction model prefers plain text, so a data-conversion step is needed in between to turn the OCR result into the target format.
102: When selecting models, do not look only at one model's quality; also check whether it fits the whole pipeline. A model that tests well on its own may be awkward in a real system if its output format is hard to hand off to others.
